summary: Presents results of a survey of LDP implementations, offered to support advancing LDP through the standards process. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A questionnaire to different makers about how their versions work.

subtitle: Survey results showing how different vendors implemented the Label Distribution Protocol.

tldr.problem: The IETF needed to assess how well different vendors had implemented LDP before advancing it to Draft Standard, particularly to verify interoperability and feature coverage.
tldr.mechanism: A detailed implementation survey was sent to vendors in August 2002, asking which LDP features they implemented and whether they had tested each feature against independent implementations. The survey covered interface types, label spaces, discovery mechanisms, modes, and all message types and TLVs.
tldr.outcome: Twelve vendor implementations responded, showing comprehensive feature coverage, strong interoperability, and solid evidence that LDP was ready for standards advancement. Every feature was implemented by at least 2 vendors, and most core features had near-universal testing.

today: RFC 5038 provided the implementation survey evidence that supported LDP's advancement to Draft Standard. LDP has since been updated in RFC 5036 and remains the standard for label distribution in MPLS networks that do not require traffic engineering.

sections.title: Why the Maturity Survey Matters
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) requires that Label Switching Routers (LSRs) agree on the meaning of labels so they can forward traffic consistently. The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) is the standard procedure by which one LSR tells another what label bindings it has made. LDP was originally specified in RFC 3036 but was evaluated as Proposed Standard.

Before LDP could advance to Draft Standard, it needed to demonstrate that vendors had implemented it correctly and that implementations could work together. This RFC presents the results of an August 2002 survey of 12 LDP implementations, which provided evidence of interoperability and maturity.
sections.eli5: Network equipment vendors were asked if they all built a routing feature the same way. If they did, they could use each other's equipment together.

sections.title: How the Survey Was Conducted
sections.content:
Twelve vendor implementations responded to the survey. Ten were available as products and two were in beta. Eleven implementations were available for purchase; one had been done by a company no longer in business. Seven implementations were written independently from the RFC; four combined purchased or free code with vendor-written code; and one was fully purchased code ported to the vendor's platform.

For each of 30 major LDP features, vendors indicated whether they had: tested the feature against another independent implementation ('t'), implemented it but not tested it ('y'), not implemented it ('n'), or found it not applicable ('x'). Vendors could optionally explain why they did not implement a feature (unclear spec, unclear utility, or not required).
sections.eli5: The survey asked vendors simple questions: Did you build this? Did you test it against someone else's version? Every vendor answered about every part of the protocol.

sections.title: What the Results Showed
sections.content:
Every LDP feature in the survey questionnaire was implemented by at least 2 vendors. Core features showed near-universal implementation and testing. For example, all 12 vendors implemented packet interface types, basic LDP discovery, basic and targeted sessions, and the core Hello, Initialization, KeepAlive, and Label Mapping messages. Most vendors tested these features against other implementations.

More specialized features showed lower adoption. Frame Relay and ATM interfaces were tested by only 2 and 6 vendors respectively. TCP MD5 security option was tested by only 3 vendors, with 8 not implementing it. IPv6 transport addressing was implemented by only 3 vendors. However, vendors explained most non-implementations as 'not required for our use case' rather than confusion or poor specifications, suggesting the specifications were clear even for features not every vendor needed.
sections.eli5: Everyone built the basic routing parts the same way. Special features for older network types or extra security were less common, but vendors could choose not to build them.

sections.title: Interoperability Verdict
sections.content:
All LDP Label Distribution Modes (8 combinations of Downstream/Downstream-on-Demand, Independent/Ordered control, and Liberal/Conservative label retention) were tested and implemented by at least 4 vendors. The Downstream Unsolicited with Ordered Control and Liberal label retention mode was tested by 8 vendors.

The strong interoperability testing results, combined with the clear specifications (as evidenced by few complaints about clarity), supported LDP's advancement. The survey demonstrated that vendors had independently built compatible implementations of a complex protocol, which is the gold standard for evidence of specification clarity and implementation maturity.
sections.eli5: Different vendors used the protocol in different ways, and they all worked together. That proved the specification was good and everyone understood it the same way.
